title: Tao Te Ching
author: Lao Tzu
blurb: Eighty-one tiny poems on the Way: soft beats hard, empty is useful, the leader who leads least leads best.

tao.m: 'The Way' — the natural flow behind everything.
tao.e: Gardeners who work with the seasons follow the Tao of plants.

sage.e: Villagers went to the sage for advice.

nave.m: The centre of a wheel where the spokes meet.

obscurity.e: After retiring, the famous actor lived in obscurity.

excellence.e: The restaurant is known for its excellence.

discerning.e: A discerning buyer checks reviews first.

moderation.e: Eating sweets in moderation is fine.

contentment.m: Being satisfied with what you have.
contentment.e: She found contentment in small daily pleasures.

cards.title: The Tao that can't be named
cards.text: The book opens with a puzzle: the true Way cannot be fully spoken. Any name we give it is a label, not the thing itself. Lao Tzu is warning us — words point at wisdom, but living it is something else.
cards.quote: The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao.
cards.qMean: Any Way you can fully describe is not the deepest, everlasting Way.
cards.qLife: No recipe can fully capture how your mother's dal tastes.
cards.orig:
Translated by James Legge

PART 1.

Ch. 1. 1. The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao. The name that can be named is not the enduring and unchanging name.

2. (Conceived of as) having no name, it is the Originator of heaven and earth; (conceived of as) having a name, it is the Mother of all things.

3.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: Chinese landscape fan painting · public domain

cards.title: Beauty needs ugliness
cards.text: The moment everyone agrees what is beautiful, they also create the idea of ugly. Good and bad, hard and easy, long and short all exist only in relation to each other. So the sage doesn't cling to one side.
cards.quote: All in the world know the beauty of the beautiful
cards.qMean: Calling something beautiful creates the idea of ugliness too.
cards.qLife: Calling one child 'the clever one' quietly labels the others.
cards.orig:
2. 1. All in the world know the beauty of the beautiful, and in doing this they have (the idea of) what ugliness is; they all know the skill of the skilful, and in doing this they have (the idea of) what the want of skill is.

2. So it is that existence and non-existence give birth the one to (the idea of) the other; that difficulty and ease produce the one (the idea of) the other; that length and shortness fashion out the one the figure of the other; that (the ideas of) height and lowness arise from the contrast of the one with the other; that the musical notes and tones become harmonious through the relation of one with another; and that being before and behind give the idea of one following another.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: Min Zhen - Landscape in the Manner of Ma Yuan · public domain

cards.title: The empty bowl
cards.text: The Way is like an empty bowl that never needs filling. However much you draw from it, it never runs out, and it never overflows. Usefulness comes from emptiness, not fullness.
cards.quote: The Tao is (like) the emptiness of a vessel
cards.qMean: The Way is like an empty bowl that is always useful.
cards.qLife: An open mind can take in more than a mind already full of opinions.
cards.orig:
4. 1. The Tao is (like) the emptiness of a vessel; and in our employment of it we must be on our guard against all fulness. How deep and unfathomable it is, as if it were the Honoured Ancestor of all things!

2. We should blunt our sharp points, and unravel the complications of things; we should attemper our brightness, and bring ourselves into agreement with the obscurity of others. How pure and still the Tao is, as if it would ever so continue!
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: Hare's fur Tea bowl Song Dynasty Musée Mariemont 08112015 1 · public domain

cards.title: Put yourself last
cards.text: The sage puts himself last and ends up first; he forgets himself and is kept safe. Because he has no selfish aims, his real aims are achieved.
cards.quote: Therefore the sage puts his own person last, and yet it is found in the foremost place
cards.qMean: The wise person puts themselves last, and ends up ahead.
cards.qLife: A captain who passes the ball and lets others score becomes the team's leader.
cards.orig:
2. Therefore the sage puts his own person last, and yet it is found in the foremost place; he treats his person as if it were foreign to him, and yet that person is preserved. Is it not because he has no personal and private ends, that therefore such ends are realised?

8. 1. The highest excellence is like (that of) water. The excellence of water appears in its benefiting all things, and in its occupying, without striving (to the contrary), the low place which all men dislike. Hence (its way) is near to (that of) the Tao.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: Portrait of a Chinese sage · public domain

cards.title: The highest good is like water
cards.text: Water helps all things and fights with none. It flows to the low places that people avoid. Lao Tzu's ideal is just as humble, useful and patient.
cards.quote: The highest excellence is like (that of) water.
cards.qMean: The best kind of goodness is like water — helpful and humble.
cards.qLife: A colleague who quietly helps everyone and never competes for credit.
cards.orig:
8. 1. The highest excellence is like (that of) water. The excellence of water appears in its benefiting all things, and in its occupying, without striving (to the contrary), the low place which all men dislike. Hence (its way) is near to (that of) the Tao.

2. The excellence of a residence is in (the suitability of) the place; that of the mind is in abysmal stillness; that of associations is in their being with the virtuous; that of government is in its securing good order; that of (the conduct of) affairs is in its ability; and that of (the initiation of) any movement is in its timeliness.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: The Waterfall · public domain

cards.title: Step back when it's done
cards.text: Fill a bowl to the brim and it spills; sharpen a blade too much and it breaks. When the work is done and your name is known, step back. That is the way of Heaven.
cards.quote: When the work is done, and one's name is becoming distinguished, to withdraw into obscurity is the way of Heaven.
cards.qMean: When the job's done and you're getting famous, quietly step aside.
cards.qLife: A founder who hands the company to new leaders at its peak.
cards.orig:
2. When gold and jade fill the hall, their possessor cannot keep them safe. When wealth and honours lead to arrogancy, this brings its evil on itself. When the work is done, and one's name is becoming distinguished, to withdraw into obscurity is the way of Heaven.

10. 1. When the intelligent and animal souls are held together in one embrace, they can be kept from separating. When one gives undivided attention to the (vital) breath, and brings it to the utmost degree of pliancy, he can become as a (tender) babe. When he has cleansed away the most mysterious sights (of his imagination), he can become without a flaw.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: Xu Yang - Hermit's cottage in the mountains · public domain

cards.title: Empty is useful
cards.text: Thirty spokes meet at the hub, but the hole in the middle makes the wheel work. A pot is useful because it is hollow; a room because of its empty space. What isn't there matters as much as what is.
cards.quote: The thirty spokes unite in the one nave; but it is on the empty space (for the axle), that the use of the wheel depends.
cards.qMean: A wheel works because of the empty space at its centre.
cards.qLife: A calendar with free time in it is what lets you handle surprises.
cards.orig: 11. The thirty spokes unite in the one nave; but it is on the empty space (for the axle), that the use of the wheel depends. Clay is fashioned into vessels; but it is on their empty hollowness, that their use depends. The door and windows are cut out (from the walls) to form an apartment; but it is on the empty space (within), that its use depends. Therefore, what has a (positive) existence serves for profitable adaptation, and what has not that for (actual) usefulness.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: Chariot Wheel with Bronze Hub, Tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng · public domain
cards.link: Part One met the nameless Way and its first image, water. Part Two turns to emptiness and stillness.

cards.title: Praise and blame alike
cards.text: Being praised and being disgraced should both make us uneasy, because both tie us to other people's opinions. Care too much about honour and you will fear losing it.
cards.quote: Favour and disgrace would seem equally to be feared
cards.qMean: Both praise and shame should be treated with caution.
cards.qLife: Someone who lives for likes is shaken by every bad comment.
cards.orig:
13. 1. Favour and disgrace would seem equally to be feared; honour and great calamity, to be regarded as personal conditions (of the same kind).

2. What is meant by speaking thus of favour and disgrace? Disgrace is being in a low position (after the enjoyment of favour). The getting that (favour) leads to the apprehension (of losing it), and the losing it leads to the fear of (still greater calamity):--this is what is meant by saying that favour and disgrace would seem equally to be feared.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: Ming Yingzong (1) · public domain

cards.title: Return to the root
cards.text: Make your mind as still as possible. Then you can watch all things rise, flourish and return to their roots. Returning to the root is peace.
cards.quote: All things alike go through their processes of activity, and (then) we see them return (to their original state).
cards.qMean: Everything goes through its life and then returns to where it began.
cards.qLife: Leaves fall in autumn and feed the same tree in spring.
cards.orig: 16. 1. The (state of) vacancy should be brought to the utmost degree, and that of stillness guarded with unwearying vigour. All things alike go through their processes of activity, and (then) we see them return (to their original state). When things (in the vegetable world) have displayed their luxuriant growth, we see each of them return to its root. This returning to their root is what we call the state of stillness; and that stillness may be called a reporting that they have fulfilled their appointed end.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: China, Southern Song dynasty - Bird on a Flowering Branch · public domain

cards.title: The best leaders are barely noticed
cards.text: The best rulers are hardly known by their people. Next come those loved and praised, then those feared, then those despised. When the best leader's work is done, the people say: we did it ourselves.
cards.quote: Their work was done and their undertakings were successful, while the people all said, 'We are as we are, of ourselves!'
cards.qMean: When good leaders succeed, people feel they did it themselves.
cards.qLife: A coach whose team believes the win was all theirs.
cards.orig:
2. How irresolute did those (earliest rulers) appear, showing (by their reticence) the importance which they set upon their words! Their work was done and their undertakings were successful, while the people all said, 'We are as we are, of ourselves!'

18. 1. When the Great Tao (Way or Method) ceased to be observed, benevolence and righteousness came into vogue. (Then) appeared wisdom and shrewdness, and there ensued great hypocrisy.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: Xu Yang - Village school · public domain

cards.title: When the Way is lost
cards.text: Only when the great Way is forgotten do people start preaching kindness and duty. Rules appear when natural goodness is gone, and cleverness brings hypocrisy with it.
cards.quote: When the Great Tao (Way or Method) ceased to be observed, benevolence and righteousness came into vogue.
cards.qMean: People talk about being good only once natural goodness is lost.
cards.qLife: Families that trust each other don't need written house rules.
cards.orig:
18. 1. When the Great Tao (Way or Method) ceased to be observed, benevolence and righteousness came into vogue. (Then) appeared wisdom and shrewdness, and there ensued great hypocrisy.

2. When harmony no longer prevailed throughout the six kinships, filial sons found their manifestation; when the states and clans fell into disorder, loyal ministers appeared.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: Cropped version of Confucius Portrait, Kongzi (Confucius) Family Mansion, Qufu · public domain

cards.title: Bend to be whole
cards.text: What is partial becomes complete; what is bent becomes straight; what is empty is filled. The sage doesn't show off, so he shines; doesn't boast, so he is respected.
cards.quote: The partial becomes complete; the crooked, straight; the empty, full
cards.qMean: What seems incomplete or crooked can become whole and straight.
cards.qLife: A humble beginner often ends up the most skilled.
cards.orig:
22. 1. The partial becomes complete; the crooked, straight; the empty, full; the worn out, new. He whose (desires) are few gets them; he whose (desires) are many goes astray.

2. Therefore the sage holds in his embrace the one thing (of humility), and manifests it to all the world. He is free from self-display, and therefore he shines; from self-assertion, and therefore he is distinguished; from self-boasting, and therefore his merit is acknowledged; from self-complacency, and therefore he acquires superiority. It is because he is thus free from striving that therefore no one in the world is able to strive with him.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.link: Stillness lets things return to their roots. Part Three shows how bending and yielding make things whole.
cards.cap: Xia Chang - Bamboo in Wind · public domain

cards.title: Storms don't last
cards.text: A whirlwind doesn't last all morning; a cloudburst doesn't last all day. If even heaven and earth can't keep up violent bursts, how could people?
cards.quote: If Heaven and Earth cannot make such (spasmodic) actings last long, how much less can man!
cards.qMean: Nothing violent or sudden lasts long, especially for people.
cards.qLife: Crash diets end quickly; steady habits stay.
cards.orig: 23. 1. Abstaining from speech marks him who is obeying the spontaneity of his nature. A violent wind does not last for a whole morning; a sudden rain does not last for the whole day. To whom is it that these (two) things are owing? To Heaven and Earth. If Heaven and Earth cannot make such (spasmodic) actings last long, how much less can man!
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: Lop Nur, Xinjiang, China · public domain

cards.title: Weight steadies the light
cards.text: Heaviness is the root of lightness; stillness rules over restlessness. A wise ruler, travelling all day, never leaves his supply wagons. Don't let showy prospects pull you from your base.
cards.quote: Gravity is the root of lightness; stillness, the ruler of movement
cards.qMean: Seriousness grounds frivolity; calm controls restlessness.
cards.qLife: A calm parent keeps a hectic household steady.
cards.orig:
26. 1. Gravity is the root of lightness; stillness, the ruler of movement.

2. Therefore a wise prince, marching the whole day, does not go far from his baggage waggons. Although he may have brilliant prospects to look at, he quietly remains (in his proper place), indifferent to them. How should the lord of a myriad chariots carry himself lightly before the kingdom? If he do act lightly, he has lost his root (of gravity); if he proceed to active movement, he will lose his throne.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: Paintings on east wall of Xu Xianxiu Tomb · public domain

cards.title: No tracks left
cards.text: A skilled traveller leaves no wheel ruts; a skilled speaker makes no slips. The sage is good at saving people, and so casts no one away.
cards.quote: The skilful traveller leaves no traces of his wheels or footsteps
cards.qMean: True skill leaves no visible trace.
cards.qLife: A great editor's work is invisible in a smooth book.
cards.orig: 27. 1. The skilful traveller leaves no traces of his wheels or footsteps; the skilful speaker says nothing that can be found fault with or blamed; the skilful reckoner uses no tallies; the skilful closer needs no bolts or bars, while to open what he has shut will be impossible; the skilful binder uses no strings or knots, while to unloose what he has bound will be impossible. In the same way the sage is always skilful at saving men, and so he does not cast away any man; he is always skilful at saving things, and so he does not cast away anything. This is called 'Hiding the light of his procedure.'
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: Fan K'uan 002 · public domain

cards.title: Grab it and lose it
cards.text: Whoever tries to seize the world and shape it to their will fails. The world is a sacred vessel; grasp it and you lose it.
cards.quote: He who would so win it destroys it; he who would hold it in his grasp loses it.
cards.qMean: Trying to control everything destroys what you wanted.
cards.qLife: A controlling friend who loses the friendship by clinging.
cards.orig:
2. The unwrought material, when divided and distributed, forms vessels. The sage, when employed, becomes the Head of all the Officers (of government); and in his greatest regulations he employs no violent measures.

29. 1. If any one should wish to get the kingdom for himself, and to effect this by what he does, I see that he will not succeed. The kingdom is a spirit-like thing, and cannot be got by active doing. He who would so win it destroys it; he who would hold it in his grasp loses it.

2.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: Warring States Banquet Hall with Bronze Ritual Vessels · public domain

cards.title: Weapons are unlucky
cards.text: Even beautiful weapons are instruments of ill omen. The wise use them only when there is no choice, and mourn even a victory, because it was paid for in lives.
cards.quote: Now arms, however beautiful, are instruments of evil omen
cards.qMean: Weapons, however fine, bring bad fortune.
cards.qLife: Winning a bitter argument can still cost a friendship.
cards.orig:
31. 1. Now arms, however beautiful, are instruments of evil omen, hateful, it may be said, to all creatures. Therefore they who have the Tao do not like to employ them.

2. The superior man ordinarily considers the left hand the most honourable place, but in time of war the right hand. Those sharp weapons are instruments of evil omen, and not the instruments of the superior man;--he uses them only on the compulsion of necessity. Calm and repose are what he prizes; victory (by force of arms) is to him undesirable. To consider this desirable would be to delight in the slaughter of men; and he who delights in the slaughter of men cannot get his will in the kingdom.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.link: Yielding is not weakness. Part Four is about how the soft overcomes the hard, even in war.
cards.cap: Ancient Chinese Writing on Spring & Autumn Bronze Jian (Sword) of Goujian (Copy) · public domain

cards.title: Mastering yourself
cards.text: Knowing others is cleverness; knowing yourself is wisdom. Beating others shows strength; beating your own habits shows real power. Being content is being rich.
cards.quote: He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is intelligent.
cards.qMean: Understanding others is clever; understanding yourself is wise.
cards.qLife: Knowing you get cranky when hungry, and eating before the big meeting.
cards.orig:
33. 1. He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is intelligent. He who overcomes others is strong; he who overcomes himself is mighty. He who is satisfied with his lot is rich; he who goes on acting with energy has a (firm) will.

2. He who does not fail in the requirements of his position, continues long; he who dies and yet does not perish, has longevity.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: William Alexander - A Young Chinese Scholar · public domain

cards.title: Rich with enough
cards.text: Whoever is content with what they have is rich. Whoever keeps going with energy has a firm will. Whoever stays true to their place lasts long.
cards.quote: He who is satisfied with his lot is rich
cards.qMean: Being satisfied with what you have is true wealth.
cards.qLife: Enjoying your old phone instead of craving the newest one.
cards.orig:
33. 1. He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is intelligent. He who overcomes others is strong; he who overcomes himself is mighty. He who is satisfied with his lot is rich; he who goes on acting with energy has a (firm) will.

2. He who does not fail in the requirements of his position, continues long; he who dies and yet does not perish, has longevity.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: Chen Hongshou - Paintings after Ancient Masters, Scholars in a Garden · public domain

cards.title: Soft beats hard
cards.text: To shrink something, first let it expand; to weaken it, first let it grow strong. Lao Tzu's lesson: the soft overcomes the hard, the weak the strong.
cards.quote: The soft overcomes the hard; and the weak the strong.
cards.qMean: Gentleness ends up beating force.
cards.qLife: A patient listener calms an angry customer better than an argument.
cards.orig:
36. 1. When one is about to take an inspiration, he is sure to make a (previous) expiration; when he is going to weaken another, he will first strengthen him; when he is going to overthrow another, he will first have raised him up; when he is going to despoil another, he will first have made gifts to him:--this is called 'Hiding the light (of his procedure).'

2. The soft overcomes the hard; and the weak the strong.

3. Fishes should not be taken from the deep; instruments for the profit of a state should not be shown to the people.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: Scholar looking at a waterfall MET DT6780 · public domain

cards.title: Doing nothing, leaving nothing undone
cards.text: The Way never forces anything, yet nothing is left undone. If rulers could keep to it, everything would transform by itself.
cards.quote: The Tao in its regular course does nothing (for the sake of doing it), and so there is nothing which it does not do.
cards.qMean: The Way doesn't force things, yet everything gets done.
cards.qLife: A good garden mostly grows itself if the soil is right.
cards.orig:
3. Fishes should not be taken from the deep; instruments for the profit of a state should not be shown to the people.

37. 1. The Tao in its regular course does nothing (for the sake of doing it), and so there is nothing which it does not do.

2. If princes and kings were able to maintain it, all things would of themselves be transformed by them.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: ·· · public domain

cards.title: If they didn't laugh
cards.text: When the best scholars hear of the Way, they practise it. Average ones half believe. The worst laugh out loud. If they didn't laugh, it wouldn't be the Way.
cards.quote: If it were not (thus) laughed at, it would not be fit to be the Tao.
cards.qMean: Deep truths often sound ridiculous to shallow minds.
cards.qLife: Great ideas are often mocked before they're accepted.
cards.orig: 41. 1. Scholars of the highest class, when they hear about the Tao, earnestly carry it into practice. Scholars of the middle class, when they have heard about it, seem now to keep it and now to lose it. Scholars of the lowest class, when they have heard about it, laugh greatly at it. If it were not (thus) laughed at, it would not be fit to be the Tao.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.link: Lao Tzu now turns to the second half of his book, on Te, the power that comes from living the Way.
cards.cap: Seigan Sōi - Budai - 2015.79.176 - Minneapolis Institute of Art · public domain

cards.title: Lose to gain
cards.text: Sometimes things grow by being reduced and shrink by being increased. The violent and strong rarely die a natural death.
cards.quote: some things are increased by being diminished
cards.qMean: Giving something up can leave you with more.
cards.qLife: Saying no to some commitments gives you more time for what matters.
cards.orig:
2. What men dislike is to be orphans, to have little virtue, to be as carriages without naves; and yet these are the designations which kings and princes use for themselves. So it is that some things are increased by being diminished, and others are diminished by being increased.

3. What other men (thus) teach, I also teach. The violent and strong do not die their natural death. I will make this the basis of my teaching.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: Zhang Ruoai - Desk Album, Flower and Bird Paintings (Bird with Plum Blossoms) - 1967.193.j - Cleveland Museum of Art · public domain

cards.title: Enough is enough
cards.text: When the Way rules, war-horses pull manure carts on the farms. When it's lost, war-horses breed at the borders. Knowing when you have enough is the only lasting sufficiency.
cards.quote: the sufficiency of contentment is an enduring and unchanging sufficiency
cards.qMean: Being content is the only 'enough' that lasts.
cards.qLife: Stopping eating when full instead of when the plate is empty.
cards.orig:
2. There is no guilt greater than to sanction ambition; no calamity greater than to be discontented with one's lot; no fault greater than the wish to be getting. Therefore the sufficiency of contentment is an enduring and unchanging sufficiency.

47. 1. Without going outside his door, one understands (all that takes place) under the sky; without looking out from his window, one sees the Tao of Heaven. The farther that one goes out (from himself), the less he knows.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: Painting of horse by Han Gan as catalogued in Shiqu Baoji · public domain

cards.title: Understand without going out
cards.text: Without leaving home you can understand the world; without looking out the window you can see the Way of heaven. The farther you go, the less you know.
cards.quote: The farther that one goes out (from himself), the less he knows.
cards.qMean: Chasing far away often teaches less than looking within.
cards.qLife: Travelling the world won't fix what you avoid facing at home.
cards.orig:
47. 1. Without going outside his door, one understands (all that takes place) under the sky; without looking out from his window, one sees the Tao of Heaven. The farther that one goes out (from himself), the less he knows.

2. Therefore the sages got their knowledge without travelling; gave their (right) names to things without seeing them; and accomplished their ends without any purpose of doing so.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: The Cassia Grove Studio · public domain

cards.title: Good to all
cards.text: The sage is good to those who are good and also to those who are not, and so everyone becomes good. He trusts the trustworthy and the untrustworthy, and trust spreads.
cards.quote: To those who are good (to me), I am good; and to those who are not good (to me), I am also good
cards.qMean: Be kind even to those who aren't kind to you.
cards.qLife: Greeting a grumpy neighbour warmly every morning.
cards.orig:
2. To those who are good (to me), I am good; and to those who are not good (to me), I am also good;--and thus (all) get to be good. To those who are sincere (with me), I am sincere; and to those who are not sincere (with me), I am also sincere;--and thus (all) get to be sincere.

3. The sage has in the world an appearance of indecision, and keeps his mind in a state of indifference to all. The people all keep their eyes and ears directed to him, and he deals with them all as his children.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: One Hundred Children Playing in the Spring · public domain

cards.title: Strong means old
cards.text: A newborn is soft yet holds tight, cries all day without going hoarse. When things become hard and strong, they begin to age. Forcing strength is against the Way.
cards.quote: When things have become strong, they (then) become old
cards.qMean: When things grow rigid and strong, they start to decline.
cards.qLife: A company that stops changing once it's big starts to fall behind.
cards.orig:
To him by whom this harmony is known, (The secret of) the unchanging (Tao) is shown, And in the knowledge wisdom finds its throne. All life-increasing arts to evil turn; Where the mind makes the vital breath to burn, (False) is the strength, (and o'er it we should mourn.)

4. When things have become strong, they (then) become old, which may be said to be contrary to the Tao. Whatever is contrary to the Tao soon ends.

56. 1. He who knows (the Tao) does not (care to) speak (about it); he who is (ever ready to) speak about it does not know it.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.link: Contentment is real power. Part Six asks what that means for rulers.
cards.cap: One Hundred Children in the Long Spring-crop · public domain

cards.title: Those who know don't say
cards.text: People who truly understand the Way rarely lecture about it; people who talk about it constantly usually don't understand it.
cards.quote: He who knows (the Tao) does not (care to) speak (about it); he who is (ever ready to) speak about it does not know it.
cards.qMean: Those who really know don't brag; those who brag don't really know.
cards.qLife: The best cook in the family just cooks; the one who talks endlessly about food burns the rice.
cards.orig:
56. 1. He who knows (the Tao) does not (care to) speak (about it); he who is (ever ready to) speak about it does not know it.

2. He (who knows it) will keep his mouth shut and close the portals (of his nostrils). He will blunt his sharp points and unravel the complications of things; he will attemper his brightness, and bring himself into agreement with the obscurity (of others). This is called 'the Mysterious Agreement.'
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: The Eighteen Scholars by an anonymous Ming artist 3 · public domain

cards.title: Rule by doing less
cards.text: The more rules and bans, the poorer the people; the more weapons, the more chaos. The sage says: I do nothing on purpose, and the people change by themselves.
cards.quote: I will do nothing (of purpose), and the people will be transformed of themselves
cards.qMean: If I don't force things, people improve on their own.
cards.qLife: Fewer pointless school rules can mean better behaviour.
cards.orig: 3. Therefore a sage has said, 'I will do nothing (of purpose), and the people will be transformed of themselves; I will be fond of keeping still, and the people will of themselves become correct. I will take no trouble about it, and the people will of themselves become rich; I will manifest no ambition, and the people will of themselves attain to the primitive simplicity.'
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: Lu Wenying - River Village in a Rainstorm · public domain

cards.title: Moderation
cards.text: For ruling people and serving heaven, nothing beats moderation. Holding back early builds up a reserve of strength that overcomes everything.
cards.quote: there is nothing like moderation
cards.qMean: Nothing is better than moderation.
cards.qLife: Saving a little energy for the end of a long race.
cards.orig:
59. 1. For regulating the human (in our constitution) and rendering the (proper) service to the heavenly, there is nothing like moderation.

2. It is only by this moderation that there is effected an early return (to man's normal state). That early return is what I call the repeated accumulation of the attributes (of the Tao). With that repeated accumulation of those attributes, there comes the subjugation (of every obstacle to such return). Of this subjugation we know not what shall be the limit; and when one knows not what the limit shall be, he may be the ruler of a state.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: · Tea Fighting Southern Song dynasty · public domain

cards.title: Govern gently
cards.text: Ruling a big country is like cooking small fish: poke and stir too much and they fall apart. A good ruler interferes as little as possible.
cards.quote: Governing a great state is like cooking small fish.
cards.qMean: Running a big country needs a light touch, like frying small fish.
cards.qLife: A manager who micromanages every email breaks the team's flow.
cards.orig:
60. 1. Governing a great state is like cooking small fish.

2. Let the kingdom be governed according to the Tao, and the manes of the departed will not manifest their spiritual energy. It is not that those manes have not that spiritual energy, but it will not be employed to hurt men. It is not that it could not hurt men, but neither does the ruling sage hurt them.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: Chinese fish painting · public domain

cards.title: Great things, small steps
cards.text: Deal with the hard while it's easy; do great things while they're small. The sage never tries to do anything great, and so achieves greatness.
cards.quote: Therefore the sage, while he never does what is great, is able on that account to accomplish the greatest things.
cards.qMean: By doing small things well, the wise achieve great things.
cards.qLife: Writing one page a day finishes a book.
cards.orig: 2. (The master of it) anticipates things that are difficult while they are easy, and does things that would become great while they are small. All difficult things in the world are sure to arise from a previous state in which they were easy, and all great things from one in which they were small. Therefore the sage, while he never does what is great, is able on that account to accomplish the greatest things.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.link: The quiet ruler acts early and small. Part Seven is about great things done through small steps.
cards.cap: · public domain

cards.title: Easy promises
cards.text: Someone who promises lightly rarely keeps faith; someone who thinks everything easy finds everything hard. The sage treats things as difficult, and so never meets difficulty.
cards.quote: He who lightly promises is sure to keep but little faith
cards.qMean: People who promise easily often don't deliver.
cards.qLife: The friend who says yes to everything and turns up for nothing.
cards.orig:
3. He who lightly promises is sure to keep but little faith; he who is continually thinking things easy is sure to find them difficult. Therefore the sage sees difficulty even in what seems easy, and so never has any difficulties.

64. 1. That which is at rest is easily kept hold of; before a thing has given indications of its presence, it is easy to take measures against it; that which is brittle is easily broken; that which is very small is easily dispersed. Action should be taken before a thing has made its appearance; order should be secured before disorder has begun.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: Kano Tan’yū - Four Elders of Mt. Shang · public domain

cards.title: A thousand miles, one step
cards.text: Big things grow from small beginnings: a giant tree from a sprout, a tower from a heap of earth, a long journey from a single step. Handle problems while they are small.
cards.quote: the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step.
cards.qMean: Every long journey begins with one small step.
cards.qLife: Writing one page today is how a whole book gets written.
cards.orig:
2. The tree which fills the arms grew from the tiniest sprout; the tower of nine storeys rose from a (small) heap of earth; the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step.

3. He who acts (with an ulterior purpose) does harm; he who takes hold of a thing (in the same way) loses his hold. The sage does not act (so), and therefore does no harm; he does not lay hold (so), and therefore does not lose his hold. (But) people in their conduct of affairs are constantly ruining them when they are on the eve of success. If they were careful at the end, as (they should be) at the beginning, they would not so ruin them.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: Rocky Landscape with Pines · public domain

cards.title: Before it starts
cards.text: Act before things take shape; set order before disorder begins. A tree you can't wrap your arms around grew from a tiny shoot.
cards.quote: Action should be taken before a thing has made its appearance; order should be secured before disorder has begun.
cards.qMean: Deal with problems before they appear.
cards.qLife: Fixing a small leak before it becomes a flood.
cards.orig: 64. 1. That which is at rest is easily kept hold of; before a thing has given indications of its presence, it is easy to take measures against it; that which is brittle is easily broken; that which is very small is easily dispersed. Action should be taken before a thing has made its appearance; order should be secured before disorder has begun.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: Hua Yan - Album of Landscape Paintings Illustrating Old Poems- An Old Man Sits under · public domain

cards.title: The sea is lowest
cards.text: Rivers and seas rule a hundred valleys because they lie lower than them. The sage leads by putting himself below, and since he doesn't compete, no one can compete with him.
cards.quote: Because he does not strive, no one finds it possible to strive with him.
cards.qMean: If you don't compete, no one can fight you.
cards.qLife: A humble expert people turn to instead of the loud rival.
cards.orig:
3. Therefore all in the world delight to exalt him and do not weary of him. Because he does not strive, no one finds it possible to strive with him.

67. 1. All the world says that, while my Tao is great, it yet appears to be inferior (to other systems of teaching). Now it is just its greatness that makes it seem to be inferior. If it were like any other (system), for long would its smallness have been known!
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: Admiralty Chart No 1965 Kua Lakh to Kao Tao Islands Including The Delta of the Song Ka, Published 1894, Corrections to 1926 · public domain

cards.title: Three treasures
cards.text: Lao Tzu holds three treasures: gentleness, frugality, and not daring to put himself first. Gentleness gives courage, frugality gives generosity, and humility makes a true leader.
cards.quote: I have three precious things which I prize and hold fast
cards.qMean: I keep three treasures close: gentleness, simplicity and humility.
cards.qLife: A grandparent who is kind, careful with money and never brags.
cards.orig:
2. But I have three precious things which I prize and hold fast. The first is gentleness; the second is economy; and the third is shrinking from taking precedence of others.

3. With that gentleness I can be bold; with that economy I can be liberal; shrinking from taking precedence of others, I can become a vessel of the highest honour. Now-a-days they give up gentleness and are all for being bold; economy, and are all for being liberal; the hindmost place, and seek only to be foremost;--(of all which the end is) death.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: Zhang Lu-Laozi Riding an Ox · public domain

cards.title: Knowing you don't know
cards.text: To know and think you don't know is best. Not to know and think you know is a sickness. Only by recognising it as sickness can you be free of it.
cards.quote: To know and yet (think) we do not know is the highest (attainment)
cards.qMean: The wisest know the limits of what they know.
cards.qLife: A doctor who says 'let's run another test' rather than guessing.
cards.orig:
71. 1. To know and yet (think) we do not know is the highest (attainment); not to know (and yet think) we do know is a disease.

2. It is simply by being pained at (the thought of) having this disease that we are preserved from it. The sage has not the disease. He knows the pain that would be inseparable from it, and therefore he does not have it.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.link: The book closes with its plainest words on knowledge, softness and sincerity.
cards.cap: Chen Hongshou - Paintings after Ancient Masters- Scholar Reading in a Thatched Hut by a Wat · public domain

cards.title: Heaven's net
cards.text: The net of heaven is wide and its holes are large, yet nothing slips through. Wrongdoing catches up in the end.
cards.quote: The meshes of the net of Heaven are large; far apart, but letting nothing escape.
cards.qMean: Heaven's justice seems loose but nothing escapes it.
cards.qLife: A lie that seems safe eventually comes out.
cards.orig: 2. It is the way of Heaven not to strive, and yet it skilfully overcomes; not to speak, and yet it is skilful in obtaining a reply; does not call, and yet men come to it of themselves. Its demonstrations are quiet, and yet its plans are skilful and effective. The meshes of the net of Heaven are large; far apart, but letting nothing escape.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: The fisherfolks at Chinese Fishing Nets · public domain

cards.title: Supple and alive
cards.text: At birth we are soft and supple; at death, stiff and hard. Green plants bend; dead ones snap. Stiffness belongs to death, suppleness to life.
cards.quote: Man at his birth is supple and weak; at his death, firm and strong
cards.qMean: Flexibility is a sign of life; rigidity of death.
cards.qLife: Stretching every morning to stay supple as you age.
cards.orig:
3. The people make light of dying because of the greatness of their labours in seeking for the means of living. It is this which makes them think light of dying. Thus it is that to leave the subject of living altogether out of view is better than to set a high value on it.

76. 1. Man at his birth is supple and weak; at his death, firm and strong. (So it is with) all things. Trees and plants, in their early growth, are soft and brittle; at their death, dry and withered.

2. Thus it is that firmness and strength are the concomitants of death; softness and weakness, the concomitants of life.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: Ke Jiusi - Bamboo after Wen Tong · public domain

cards.title: Knowing isn't doing
cards.text: Nothing is softer than water, yet nothing beats it at wearing away the hard. Everyone knows the soft overcomes the hard, but almost no one lives by it.
cards.quote: Every one in the world knows that the soft overcomes the hard, and the weak the strong, but no one is able to carry it out in practice.
cards.qMean: Everyone knows gentleness wins, but few practise it.
cards.qLife: Knowing shouting won't help, and shouting anyway.
cards.orig:
78. 1. There is nothing in the world more soft and weak than water, and yet for attacking things that are firm and strong there is nothing that can take precedence of it;--for there is nothing (so effectual) for which it can be changed.

2. Every one in the world knows that the soft overcomes the hard, and the weak the strong, but no one is able to carry it out in practice.

3.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
cards.cap: Ma Yuan - Water Album - The Yellow River Breaches its Course · public domain

cards.title: Sincere words
cards.text: The book ends simply: sincere words aren't pretty, pretty words aren't sincere. The wise don't argue; those who argue aren't wise. The sage keeps nothing back, and the more he gives, the more he has.
cards.quote: Sincere words are not fine; fine words are not sincere.
cards.qMean: True words are plain; fancy words are often false.
cards.qLife: A simple 'I'm sorry' means more than a long, polished excuse.
cards.orig:
81. 1. Sincere words are not fine; fine words are not sincere. Those who are skilled (in the Tao) do not dispute (about it); the disputatious are not skilled in it. Those who know (the Tao) are not extensively learned; the extensively learned do not know it.

2. The sage does not accumulate (for himself). The more that he expends for others, the more does he possess of his own; the more that he gives to others, the more does he have himself.
cards.origFrom: Lao Tzu, Tao Te Ching (tr. Legge, 1891)
